title: Children and death
hookLine: children do best with plain, honest words

lines: THE BOY WON'T GO TO BED.
WHY ISN'T ANYONE LOOKING FOR GRANDMA?
cards: A small boy is told that Grandpa went to sleep and won't wake up. That night, he won't get into bed.
He fights it, crying, and nobody can work out why, until someone finally asks him, and he says he doesn't want to go to sleep like Grandpa.

Across town, a little girl hears that the family lost Grandma, and she wants to know why nobody is out looking for her. The grown-ups chose soft words to protect them. The children took the words at their word.

teach.b: Organizations that support grieving children, such as the Dougy Center in Portland, Oregon, advise using the real words, died and dead, and explaining them in a way a child can hold: the body stopped working.
It doesn't breathe, eat, or feel pain anymore, and it can't start again. It sounds harsh to adult ears. To a child, it's something solid to stand on.
Second, why soft words can backfire. Young children can take words literally. Asleep can make bedtime frightening.
Lost suggests someone could be found. Went away can sound like a choice, or leave a child waiting at the window. The kindness meant can turn into fear or confusion.
Third, short, honest, and again. Children may ask the same question many times, sometimes days apart, and may play happily one minute and cry the next. That doesn't mean they didn't understand.
They're taking it in a bit at a time. The guidance: answer briefly and truthfully, as many times as it's asked, and say I don't know when you don't.
Fourth, beliefs beside the fact, not instead of it. Families hold different beliefs about what follows death: heaven, rebirth, a return to God, or that nobody knows.
Child grief guidance suggests sharing your family's beliefs alongside the plain fact. Grandma died. Her body stopped working.
And then: here's what our family believes. The fact first, the belief beside it.

how: Children's grief centers and hospice programs coach parents to use the words died and dead, explain that the body has stopped working, answer questions briefly and honestly, and share the family's beliefs alongside the facts.

games.q: soft word, what a child hears — tap the pairs.

s: telling a child Grandpa went to sleep is the gentlest choice
it can make bedtime frightening; children take words at their word.
it's all right to tell a child "I don't know"
the guidance is to answer briefly and truthfully, including I don't know.
families should keep their beliefs out of it
the guidance suggests sharing beliefs beside the plain fact, not instead of it.

games.q: a small child looks up at you and asks, "is Grandpa sleeping?" what do you say?
o: "yes, he's sleeping for a very long time."
"no. Grandpa died. his body stopped working."
games.why: plain words first, then stay for the next question, and the one after that. that's what grief guidance for children advises.

practice: Think of a death a child in your life might ask about, a grandparent, a neighbor, a goldfish, and quietly shape one sentence they could understand: the name, the word died, and one plain thing, like her body stopped working, so she can't come back.
Notice any urge to soften it, and let the urge pass. Then add one warm, true line, such as we loved her, and we'll keep remembering her, and rest with the two sentences together.

wordCard.voice: Dougy Center, the organization that advises telling children the truth in plain words, died and dead, with warmth and room for questions. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: plain words. To a child, the plain word is solid ground. Day eight hundred three, done.
